20% improvement in QC efficiency with a scan-first workflow

Piece Tracker is the tablet app QC checkers use to track each garment, check its quality and record every Pass, Rework and Reject piece. I redesigned the workflow with simpler size cards, progressive disclosure and QR/barcode scanning that selects the right size automatically, so checkers scroll less, select less and think less.

ProductTrendz CMP
Piece Tracker
RoleUX / Product Designer
PlatformWeb app on 8-10″ tablets
UsersQC checkers, garment inspectors
IndustryGarment manufacturing
Result20% increase in operational efficiency
+20%operational efficiency
7 → 4steps from garment to QC action
8-10″tablet, used on the factory floor
01 — The challenge

A size-first workflow that outgrew the tablet

Piece Tracker is used by QC checkers on the production floor to track each garment, check its quality and record outcomes such as Pass, Rework and Reject pieces. The checker enters information in a left-side panel, generates production data, checks the garment, finds its size on the tablet, selects it, reviews the QC information and then chooses an action.

The flow worked, but some styles had more than eight sizes. The size cards ran past the available space on 8-10″ tablets, so checkers had to scroll, find the right size, select it and only then continue. For a repetitive task, that was unnecessary interaction and effort.

02 — Understanding the user need

Check garment, identify size, take action

In discussions with QC users we learned that they were not primarily interested in the details inside every size card. The detail consumed screen space without supporting their main task. That led to two questions:

01Can we show size status without filling every card with information?
02Can we eliminate manual size searching altogether?
ScrollingLong size lists had to be navigated on a small screen.
Manual identificationThe user had to know or identify the garment size first.
Information overloadDetailed data on every card, though not needed for every inspection.
Split attentionGarment, tablet, size, details, then the action button.
03 — The insight

Overview first. Details on demand.

The size cards were doing two jobs: showing production status and providing detailed QC information. I separated them. The cards became simple status indicators, and a compact panel with the selected size's Total Qty, Checked, Pass, Reject and Rework appears only when a size is selected.

Show only what the user needs to scan. Reveal details when the user needs them.

This reduced visual noise, shrank the size grid's footprint and kept the important QC numbers one tap away.

04 — Scan, identify, act

From navigation to identification

Every garment already carries a QR/barcode. Instead of asking the checker to locate a size on the tablet, the physical garment becomes the entry point into the digital workflow.

BeforeEnter data→Scroll→Find size→Select→Check→Action
NowScan→Identify→Check→Action
01ScanThe checker scans the QR/barcode attached to the garment.
02IdentifyThe system identifies the garment and highlights its size.
03ReviewRelevant QC information appears for that size.
04ActPass, Reject or Rework, directly after the scan.

The old mental model was “Where is this garment's size?” The new one is “Scan the garment and inspect it.” On a factory-floor tablet, where a style can have XS to XXXL plus numeric sizes, removing the scroll, search, identify and tap loop for every garment matters.

05 — Supporting screens

Setup and document details

The tracker mode selected during setup (Manual or Traceability) decides whether the scan field appears. Document details stay in a side panel so the main workspace remains uncluttered.

06 — Before and after

What changed

BeforeAfter
Primary interactionSize selectionBarcode scanning
Size identificationManualAutomatic
Size cardsInformation-heavyStatus-focused
Detailed dataAlways visibleShown on selection
Multiple sizesRequired scrollingQuick visual overview
QC actionAfter navigating to a sizeDirectly after scan
Cognitive loadHigherLower
07 — Design decisions

Five decisions, each with a reason

01Simplified size cardsUsers did not need detail on every card during the primary inspection task.
02Progressive disclosureKeep the overview clean and reveal QC details for the selected size only.
03Scan-first interactionThe garment already has a unique identifier, so the system can do the identifying.
04Automatic size selectionRemoves unnecessary scrolling and manual selection.
05Direct QC actionsOnce identified, the user can complete the inspection immediately.
08 — Impact

Efficiency gain from many small optimizations

+20%

increase in operational efficiency, from reduced size-card complexity, less scrolling, less manual size searching, automatic garment identification, progressive disclosure of QC information and faster access to QC actions.

Success metrics used to validate the design

Time to QC actionGarment pickup to Pass, Reject or Rework.
Size search timeTime spent locating the correct size.
Interactions per garmentTaps and actions per inspection.
Scan success rateGarments identified on the first scan.
Manual selection errorsIncorrect size selections before action.
Garments per hourOverall QC throughput.
09 — Outcome

From a size-driven interface to a garment-driven workflow

Show the garment to the interface, instead of finding it in the interface.

The size grid still gives the production overview, but it no longer forces operators to navigate every size for every garment. The result is a simpler tablet experience built around the physical workflow of QC operators.

One organised, clubbed-trip system for 20+ factories

A mobile app and web dashboard that turned scattered, phone-and-spreadsheet cab booking across 20+ garment factories into a single system where overlapping requests are merged into shared rides.

ClientClassic Fashion Apparel Industry
RoleUX/UI designer: research, flows, wireframes, UI
PlatformsMobile app (staff, guests, drivers) and web dashboard (admins)
-30%vehicle trips from clubbing passengers
15-30fewer trips every day
450-900fewer trips per month
01 — The problem

Duplicated trips nobody could see

Classic Fashion runs more than 20 factories in different places. Moving people and goods between them is a daily, high-volume job: staff and executives travelling between sites, international guests going to hotels and airports, and garments or samples moving by road. The fleet is mixed: cars, mini buses, vans, pick-ups and lorries.

Booking was manual, by phone and spreadsheet. Nobody could see who else was travelling the same route, so a car would leave to collect one person while another took a colleague along the same road. With 50-100 trips a day, every duplicate added fuel, driver hours and vehicle wear, and nobody could see the running cost.

Factories20+in different locations
Trips per day50-100before the app
Longest inter-factory trip300+ km
Typical airport run180 km
02 — Users and needs

Three users, one shared trip record

Employee or guestRequest a cab for themselves or a group, including women and children, for a site, airport or hotel trip.Pain: calling around, no confirmation, no idea when the car arrives.
Transport adminSchedule vehicles and drivers, merge overlapping requests, watch cost.Pain: spreadsheets, no overlap check, no live view of the fleet.
DriverKnow who to pick up first and drop last.Pain: instructions by phone, unclear order of stops.
03 — Design goals

What the design had to achieve

01Book a ride in as few steps as possible
02Show admins which requests can share a vehicle, so clubbing is a one-screen decision
03Give drivers a clear pick-up and drop-off order
04Make the cost of travel visible through reports
04 — The solution

Two interfaces, one trip record

Staff and guests request on mobile, admins schedule on the web, and drivers get the ordered route on mobile.

Request→Admin reviews and clubs→Vehicle and driver assigned→Driver notified with stop order→Live tracking→Reports
1 · Mobile, staff and guestsRequesting a rideOne form covers passenger or goods, pick-up and drop-off points, times, trip type, priority and preferred vehicle. A multi pick-up and drop-off switch handles group trips. Travellers are listed with gender, nationality and self or guest, so admins know the group mix. An Allow Clubbing switch records consent to share.
2 · Web, adminsScheduling and clubbingThe home screen shows counts for requests, scheduled and completed rides above a sortable, filterable table. Admins assign a vehicle and driver, and Add Ride stacks another request onto the same vehicle. Ride numbers stay editable so pick and drop order can be corrected.
3 · Mobile, driversDriver appDrivers see the requests for the day, open one to view the requestor, vehicle, stops, return time and every passenger, then start the ride. A live map shows the route with one-tap calling to the rider.
05 — Requesting a ride

One mobile flow for passengers and goods

Wireframes settled the structure before any visual design. The annotated screens below show the decisions that matter most, and the final UI follows.

1234

New ride form

Route, dates, trip type, priority and the multi-stop switch on one screen.

  1. 1Passenger or Goods: one form serves both trip types.
  2. 2Trip type, such as Airport, sets the context for the request.
  3. 3Priority chips let requesters flag urgency.
  4. 4Multi Pickup/Drop-off switch turns the form into a group trip.
1234

Traveller review

Who is travelling, and whether they agree to share the vehicle.

  1. 1Ride summary stays visible and editable throughout.
  2. 2Traveller mix (2M, 3F, 1C, 0N) tells admins who is travelling.
  3. 3Add Passenger builds the group one traveller at a time.
  4. 4Allow Clubbing records consent to share the vehicle.
Final mobile UI
01WelcomeA calm, focused start: Smooth, Simple, Secure.
02HomeChoose Passenger or Goods and set a pickup. Upcoming rides sit below.
03Book a ridePickup, drop-off, departure and return in one card, then Go.
04Confirm ridersEach rider shows Self or Guest, with route and contact, before Confirm.
06 — Admin dashboard

Scheduling and clubbing on one screen

Admins work on a wide web dashboard: counts up top, a filterable request table, and a schedule screen where overlapping requests are stacked into one vehicle.

Dashboard

A quick read of the day, then the request table.

1234
  1. 1Status counts for requests, scheduled and completed rides, plus today's date.
  2. 2Requests and Cancelled tabs separate live work from history.
  3. 3Filter and advanced sort help admins find overlapping requests.
  4. 4The table shows vehicle type, destination and gender, the fields needed to judge clubbing.

Schedule a ride

Everything needed to assign a vehicle and driver sits on one screen.

12345
  1. 1Requestor, priority and trip type at a glance.
  2. 2Return time, with a switch to create a separate request.
  3. 3Numbered pick order (1st, 2nd, 3rd) on every passenger.
  4. 4Assign a vehicle and a driver from two selects.
  5. 5Schedule confirms the ride; Add Ride stacks another request onto it.
1234

Clubbed rides

Add Ride stacks a second request onto the same vehicle. The ride order can be edited, which keeps the pick and drop sequence correct.

  1. 1The first ride in the vehicle.
  2. 2The second ride, clubbed in. Ride numbers are editable to correct the order.
  3. 3Each ride keeps its own passengers and pick order.
  4. 4One vehicle and driver are assigned to the whole clubbed set.
07 — Driver app

A clear order of stops, one tap to act

Drivers get the day's requests, the trip detail with every passenger, and a live map, replacing instructions given over the phone.

123

Rides list

  1. 1Request count for the day, with search and filters.
  2. 2Start and one-tap call actions sit on each request.
  3. 3Club On marks rides that share a vehicle.
1234

Ride detail

  1. 1Vehicle and plate, so the driver knows what to take.
  2. 2Pick-up, drop-off and return time in one scroll.
  3. 3Passenger list with the group mix and pick order.
  4. 4Start Ride is the single primary action.
123

Live map

  1. 1The live route shows the trip in progress.
  2. 2Vehicle position updates along the route.
  3. 3One-tap call to the rider.
08 — Key design decisions

Decisions and their reasons

DecisionReason
Mobile-first for staff, web-first for adminsRequesters book on the move; admins compare many rows and need a wide table.
Traveller mix captured at request timeGender and child counts affect which trips can be safely clubbed.
Clubbing as an explicit switchKeeps requester consent clear while giving admins the option to merge.
Numbered pick order on every passengerDrivers get an unambiguous sequence instead of a phone briefing.
Neutral grey style with a blue brand accentDense operational screens stay readable; colour marks primary actions only.
09 — Results

About 30% fewer vehicle trips

Clubbing passengers into shared rides cut vehicle trips by about 30%. On 50-100 trips a day, that is roughly 15-30 fewer trips daily, or 450-900 a month. Every trip is now organised in one system, and every driver is notified of pick-up and drop-off order.

Before50-100
After35-70
Trips per day050100

How the impact is measured

MetricHow measured
Vehicle trips per dayTrip log, same weekday before and after launch
Trips organised through one systemShare of trips with an app request ID
Passengers per vehicle tripTotal passengers / total trips
Clubbed tripsTrips with 2+ requests / all trips
Cost per passenger-kmFuel and driver cost / passenger-km, from reports
Time to book a rideTimed task test with 5-8 staff
UsabilitySUS survey, target 80+
10 — What I learned

Visibility drove the saving

01Visibility, not routingOnce overlapping requests sat side by side, clubbing became an easy call for the admin.
02Consent and detailTraveller details and consent matter as much as routing when groups include women and children.
03Next stepsSuggest clubbing matches automatically by route and time window, and add cost dashboards per factory.

From breakdown calls to one connected maintenance workflow

Trendz MAC is a mobile maintenance app that links supervisors, mechanics, machines and spare parts, so every breakdown is reported with context, prepared for in advance and tracked through to verification.

ProductTrendz MAC
RoleUX / Product Designer
PlatformMobile app
UsersLine supervisors, mechanics
IndustryGarment manufacturing
ScopeBreakdown and preventive maintenance
1 hr+delay on a single breakdown before the redesign
8connected steps from request to verification
2roles working in one shared workflow
01 — The problem

Breakdowns were handled by calls and legwork

When a machine broke down, the line supervisor had to contact a mechanic and explain the issue. The mechanic then visited the machine to understand it, identified the spare parts, or searched for an alternative machine if a replacement was needed.

That meant multiple trips between the production floor, the maintenance area and the spare-parts store. A single breakdown could delay production for more than an hour.

BeforeSupervisor calls mechanic→Mechanic visits machine→Diagnoses the issue→Fetches spare parts→Or finds a replacement→Repairs
Visibility gapWhen was the request raised?
Visibility gapWhen did the mechanic start?
Visibility gapWhat caused the breakdown?
Visibility gapWhich parts or replacement machines were needed?
Visibility gapHow long did the repair take?
Visibility gapWas the machine restored to working condition?

Preventive maintenance also needed better tracking to make sure machines were serviced on time.

02 — Design goals

Four goals for the redesign

01Cut the tripsMake sure the mechanic arrives informed, so one visit does the job.
02Remove manual coordinationReplace calls and verbal explanations with a request that carries the details.
03Make maintenance visibleRecord every stage so response time, working time and history can be seen.
04Prevent the next breakdownBring preventive maintenance into the same system.
03 — The insight

Bring the information to the mechanic

The mechanic should know the problem before reaching the machine.

Most of the delay was not the repair itself but the discovery around it: understanding the issue, finding parts and finding a replacement. I designed the workflow so that discovery happens before the mechanic arrives, using the machine scan, photos and history as the source of truth.

04 — The solution

Eight steps, one connected workflow

I designed a connected workflow that lets supervisors and mechanics manage the whole maintenance process from the factory floor.

NowScan and request→Work order and notification→Scan to start→Arrive prepared→Repair or replace→Watch on dashboard→Sign off→Prevent
01Raise a request by scanningThe supervisor scans the machine. Asset ID, location and facility fill in automatically; only a title and description are required, with photos when needed.
02Request becomes a work orderSubmitting creates a work order and sends the mechanic an instant notification with the machine type, line and who raised it.
03Scan the machine to startThe mechanic goes to the line, scans the machine and swipes to start, creating a clear, timestamped start point.
04Arrive preparedImages, title and machine history show what is wrong, so the mechanic brings the right tools and spare parts, or knows the machine needs replacing.
05Repair or replaceFrom the repair screen the mechanic can hold or reject, replace the machine, or complete the repair.
06Watch it on the TV dashboardRequest and technician status, downtime and MTR show on a floor dashboard, so everyone sees which lines are affected.
07Close with a signatureA digital signature completes the repair, and the work order keeps parts, workers and tasks on record.
08Plan preventive maintenanceAsset details, history and task-based work orders support scheduled maintenance, so problems are caught before they stop a line.
05 — Key screens

The workflow, screen by screen

The process runs across two roles and one shared dashboard.

Line supervisor: raise a request

Scan the machine, add a title and description, and submit.

01HomeRequest and work order counts for the line, with the scan button at the centre of the bar.
02Scan the machineThe QR on the machine starts a new request.
03New requestAsset, location and facility fill in automatically. Title and description are mandatory; priority and photos help the mechanic.
04Request submittedSubmitting creates a work order and returns a request ID.

Mechanic: respond, repair and close

Get notified, scan to start, repair or replace, and sign off.

01NotificationMachine type, line and who raised it, with View Details and Accept.
02Work ordersEvery work order in one list, with status, category, line, station and asset.
03Scan to startScanning the machine shows its asset, location and history. Swipe to start the job.
04RepairIn-time, elapsed time and asset status, with Hold or Reject, Replace Machine and Complete Repair.
05Sign offA digital signature completes the repair.

Visibility and prevention

The TV dashboard shows the whole floor, while asset records and task-based work orders support preventive maintenance.

1234
  1. 1Status tiles count Open, Other (Assigned and Hold), In Progress and Resolved plus Rejected requests.
  2. 2Total downtime and average MTR for the facility at a glance.
  3. 3Every request shows status, technician, location, issue, MTR and downtime, so affected lines are clear.
  4. 4Technician Status shows who is available and who is busy.
01Asset detailsDetails, files, parts, requests and work orders for an asset in one place.
02Work order recordTask progress, parts consumed, workers and a digital signature on one record, which also supports preventive work.
06 — Before and after

Old way, new way

BeforeAfter
ReportingPhone call and verbal explanationMachine scan with auto-filled asset details, plus title, description and photos
Mechanic notifiedManual callInstant notification with View Details and Accept
DiagnosisOn site, after arrivingImages and title reviewed before arriving
Spare partsMultiple trips to the storeIdentified in advance
Replacement machineSearched for manuallyReplace Machine action in the repair flow
VisibilityLimitedTV dashboard shows requests, technicians, downtime and MTR
Close-outInformalDigital signature completes the work order
Preventive maintenanceHarder to trackTask-based work orders and asset history
07 — Design decisions

The thinking behind the workflow

01Scan the machineAsset ID, location and facility auto-fill, so supervisors only write a title and description.
02Mandatory title and descriptionThe minimum a mechanic needs to understand the issue before arriving.
03Instant notificationReplaces calls and manual coordination.
04Scan to startCreates a clear, timestamped start point.
05Repair or replace in one screenHold, replace or complete without leaving the work order.
06Digital signatureA clear record of who finished the job.
07TV dashboardThe whole floor sees affected lines, technician availability and downtime.
08Asset recordHistory, files, parts and work orders per asset support repair and preventive work.
08 — Impact

Faster response, fewer trips, full visibility

From a chain of calls to a single traceable workflow.

The redesign changed how breakdowns are handled on the floor. Mechanics arrive prepared, supervisors no longer chase updates by phone, and the TV dashboard shows which lines are affected, so production can recover sooner.

Fewer tripsMechanics know the issue and the parts needed before they reach the machine.
Less coordinationRequests carry the machine, photos and description, so manual calls drop away.
Clear accountabilityEvery stage is timestamped, from request and response to completion and signature.
Fewer surprisesPreventive work and asset history help teams act before downtime.

What the system now measures

MetricWhat it shows
Response timeFrom request raised to mechanic response
Working timeFrom job start to completion
Downtime and MTRTotal downtime and average repair time per facility, on the TV dashboard
Maintenance historyEvery request and repair per machine
Preventive complianceWhether scheduled tasks are done on time
09 — Outcome

From phone calls to a traceable workflow

Trendz MAC turns maintenance from a sequence of calls and trips into one mobile workflow, where the machine itself starts the process and every step is recorded through to verification.

From Excel sheets to a visual, predictive planning board

Trendz Planner turns the complexity of multi-factory production capacity into a planning system where merchandisers see capacity, planners allocate orders by drag and drop, and delivery dates are predicted before a commitment is made.

ProductTrendz Planner
RoleUX / Product Designer
PlatformWeb application
UsersMerchandisers, factory planners and managers
IndustryGarment manufacturing
Scope20+ factories, 100+ lines per factory
20+factories planned in one system
100+production lines in a single factory
7planning questions Excel made hard to answer
01 — The problem

Planning bulk orders across 20+ factories

Factories produce for global brands including Adidas, GAP, Target, Armani, American Eagle, Under Armour and Walmart. Large sales orders have to be split across factories and production lines while meeting strict delivery timelines.

A single factory can run more than 100 lines, each with different capabilities, working hours, capacity and efficiency. A line that performs well on shirts may not be as efficient on other garment categories. Planning relied on Excel and manual coordination, which made these questions hard to answer:

Q1Which factory has available capacity?
Q2Which production lines suit this order?
Q3When can a line start production?
Q4How many pieces can it produce each day?
Q5Will the planned quantity meet the delivery date?
Q6What happens if a line's efficiency drops?
Q7How should an order be redistributed when capacity changes?

As orders grew, planners kept comparing capacity, availability, efficiency and quantities by hand, which was slow and hard to maintain.

02 — The complexity

Four layers planners had to hold in their heads

Scale20+ factoriesproducing for global brands
Depth100+ linesin each factory
VariationDifferent capabilitiesworking hours, capacity and efficiency per line
DurationLong-running bulk orderswhere small changes ripple into delivery dates
03 — The insight

Plan around capacity, allocation and delivery

The question is not “is there space?” but “will this order land on time?”

Instead of designing a generic production-planning tool, I framed the product around three things planners actually need: capacity visibility, factory and line allocation, and delivery prediction. Every screen answers one of them.

MatchingOrder→Factory→Production line→Capability→Capacity
PredictionDaily output→Remaining quantity→Expected completion→Delivery status
04 — The solution

Six capabilities, one planning system

Merchandisers understand factory capacity and line capabilities, while factory managers allocate sales orders through a drag-and-drop Planning Board.

01Understand factory capacityThe Factory Board shows available slots, existing commitments, line availability and current allocation, so planners see where an order can realistically fit.
02Match orders to the right lineLine capability and efficiency, not just availability, guide the choice. A line strong on shirts becomes a clear option for a shirt order.
03Plan through drag and dropFactory managers place sales orders onto available slots and lines on the Planning Board instead of editing Excel sheets.
04Predict the delivery dateWorking hours, line capacity, historical efficiency, requirements and existing allocations produce the expected schedule automatically.
05Detect delivery risks earlyIf the planned rate cannot meet the delivery date, the system flags the risk and recalculates the schedule.
06Manage changing conditionsWhen efficiency or capacity changes, the schedule shows the effect on the final delivery date.
05 — Key screens

The boards planners work on

Three views carry the planning work: the Aerial Board for factory capacity, and the Focus Board in two orientations for line-level planning.

Aerial Board

A factory-level view of capacity over time. Planners see where an incoming order can realistically be placed before choosing a line, and the Load List brings the orders in.

123456
  1. 1Board and view switcher: the Aerial Board for factories, with Product as an alternative lens.
  2. 2Every factory is a row on one shared timeline, so capacity can be compared at a glance.
  3. 3Daily capacity bars per factory, colour-coded so loaded and open days read quickly.
  4. 4Hovering a day shows Available, Planned and Balance Qty, plus average working hours and cadre.
  5. 5Load List brings in sales orders with style, delivery date, colour, quantity, SMV and PO; rows flagged in red draw attention.
  6. 6Non-working days are shaded in the timeline, so the capacity picture stays realistic.

Focus Board: dates across the top

Line by line, with orders laid along the timeline. Dates across the top suit following a line's run over weeks and spotting where an order sits.

123456
  1. 1Toolbar for search, view and board actions, with Load List one click away.
  2. 2Lines run down the side, each with its cadre and working hours.
  3. 3Hovering a line shows its cadre, working hours and the garment categories it handles.
  4. 4Orders appear as coloured bars that span the days they occupy on a line.
  5. 5Hovering an order shows the order, product, customer, quantity and delivery date.
  6. 6Shaded columns mark non-working days, with daily figures shown in the cells.

Focus Board: dates down the side

The same plan turned on its side. Dates down the side suit comparing every line on a given day, with plan, cumulative and efficiency figures together.

123456
  1. 1A Holding area parks orders before they are placed on a line.
  2. 2Each line header carries its department, cadre, working hours and product categories.
  3. 3Line efficiency is labelled (Super, Moderate or Low efficient) and colour-coded, so a good match is easy to spot.
  4. 4Plan, cumulative and efficiency figures sit side by side for every line and day.
  5. 5Dates run down the side, with holidays marked clearly so nothing is planned on them.
  6. 6Totals close each line and the board, so the overall load is always visible.
06 — Delivery risk

Seeing the delay before it happens

Once an order sits on a line, the expected completion date is calculated from that line's capacity and efficiency. When the rate is too low, the plan shows the gap immediately.

Required delivery20 June
Projected completionPlanned run4-day delay
Required delivery20 June
Projected completion24 June
Impact4-day delay

The planner can then adjust the allocation, move the order to another line, or distribute it across available capacity, before the delay becomes a delivery issue.

07 — Before and after

Old way, new way

BeforeAfter
Capacity viewCompared by hand across sheetsFactory Board shows slots and commitments
Line selectionBased on availabilityBased on capability, efficiency and capacity
AllocationEditing Excel sheetsDrag and drop on the Planning Board
Delivery dateEstimated manuallyCalculated from capacity and efficiency
Delay detectionFound lateFlagged as soon as the plan is placed
Changes in efficiencyMultiple manual recalculationsSchedule updates to show the impact
08 — Design decisions

The thinking behind the board

01Factory-level overview firstPlanners need to know where an order can fit before choosing a line.
02Capability-aware matchingAvailability alone leads to poorly matched lines.
03Direct manipulationDragging an order onto a slot mirrors how planners already think.
04Automatic schedulingPredefined hours, capacity and efficiency remove repeated calculation.
05Risk shown at the point of decisionA delay is visible while the planner can still change the allocation.
06A plan that reactsProduction conditions change, so the schedule has to change with them.
09 — Impact

From a manual puzzle to a live plan

Real-time capacity visibility and predictive scheduling.

Each question planners used to answer by hand now has a clear answer in the product.

Planning questionWhere it is answered
Which factory has capacity?Factory Board
Which lines suit this order?Capability and efficiency matching
When can a line start, and how much can it produce daily?Line schedule and daily output
Will the order meet the delivery date?Expected completion and delivery status
What if efficiency drops or capacity changes?Recalculated schedule and delay indicator
10 — Outcome

A system planners can trust with big orders

Trendz Planner replaces Excel-based coordination with one visual workflow for understanding capacity, placing orders and predicting delivery, so adjustments happen before they become delivery problems.
